Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

I feel isolated and set apart from others

vignette:
Kiet Bùi is a twenty-two-year-old Vietnamese-American UX designer who presented for an initial psychological evaluation approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic tornado that tore through the rural Oklahoma town where he had been visiting his aunt's family over a long weekend. He had no prior history of trauma or mental health treatment, and at the time of the disaster he described himself as someone who moved through the world with relative ease - sociable, curious, absorbed in his work.

The tornado struck without adequate warning on a Saturday afternoon in early spring. Kiet had been sitting at his aunt's kitchen table eating a bowl of bún bò Huế when the sky outside the window turned a colour he later struggled to name - not green exactly, but wrong in a way that registered in his chest before his mind caught up. Within seconds the structure around him began to come apart. He was thrown from his chair and pinned beneath collapsed cabinetry for what he estimates was nearly forty minutes before emergency responders reached him. During that time he could not move his neck, could feel something warm and wet along his collarbone, and was certain, with a clarity that still disturbs him, that he was going to die alone in a stranger's kitchen. The smell of the spilled soup - star anise, lemongrass, a faint char from the gas line - was everywhere. His aunt was found in another part of the house, badly injured but alive. Two neighbours were not.

In the weeks that followed, Kiet returned to his apartment in Austin and attempted to resume his work as a UX designer at a mid-sized software firm. The physical injury to his neck had been treated, but a residual stiffness remained, and he noticed that whenever the tension in his neck flared - during long hours hunched over wireframes and prototype mockups - something would shift inside him that he could not name or contain. He would not necessarily see anything, would not replay the kitchen or the collapsed ceiling, but the full weight of that afternoon would arrive in him without an image attached to it, like a tide coming in through a door he couldn't locate. On other occasions the memory returned with a sensory precision that bewildered him: he would be sitting at his standing desk reviewing user-flow diagrams and suddenly taste star anise on the back of his tongue, sharp and unmistakable, as though the bowl were in front of him again. He found himself checking the weather application on his phone compulsively whenever he felt physically unwell - a mild headache, a wave of nausea - interpreting bodily discomfort as a signal that something catastrophic was imminent. Any news coverage of tornadoes, storm systems, or disaster relief efforts sent him immediately out of the room.

What unsettled Kiet most was not the physical intrusions but a quieter, more corrosive shift in how the world appeared to him. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally unknowable - that the warmth colleagues showed him at the office, the friendliness of his roommate, even his family's concern, concealed something unreliable beneath it. He was not sure what he expected people to reveal; he only knew that he no longer trusted the surface of things. He felt set apart from everyone around him, as though he were observing his own life through the glass of a user-testing booth - present but separated, watching behaviours he could no longer participate in naturally. The design work that had once felt collaborative and energising now required a performance of engagement he found exhausting. He stopped attending team stand-ups in person, citing audio quality, and began working almost exclusively through asynchronous messages. He had not seen friends socially in four months. What frightened him most was not any single symptom but the growing sense that there was no place - not Austin, not his family's home in San Jose, not anywhere - where he felt he still belonged. The memory of the tornado itself sometimes struck him as impossible, so extreme in its rupture of ordinary life that part of him could not fully accept that it had happened to him at all.

He sought help after his manager gently raised concerns about his withdrawal from the team, and after he found himself unable to finish a bowl of pho his roommate had made - leaving the table without explanation, unable to account for his own reaction. He came to the intake session hoping, in his words, to feel like he was part of things again.
